- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to match sentiment momentum.  
- If sentiment turns negative (e.g., < -0.5) and forecast is rising, model often overshoots — reduce forecast slope or cap upward movement.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overcorrects downward — adjust forecast to allow for mean reversion but avoid excessive drop.  
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed, model often averages out — consider smoothing or weighting recent sentiment more heavily.  
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 day pullback after peak), model tends to overpredict continuation — reduce forecast slope after peak.  
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates volatility in early part of forecast — increase initial forecast slightly if sentiment is bullish.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes, model tends to ignore them — add penalty or dampen forecast if sentiment is negative for 3+ consecutive days.
